office:text.text:p: We built a Python application, with Claude's help, that takes state logic diagrams from a GUI and generates Allen Bradley L5X code for import into Studio 5000. The current architecture is fully deterministic. Claude helped us write the Python generator once, but no AI runs at generation time. The outputcanbe inconsistent: a mix of coverage gaps (logic patterns the generator does not know how to handle), style gaps (right logic, wrong shape versus how our engineers actually write it), and difficulty with genuinely custom or complex logic that does not fit our current templates.

A purely deterministic generator cannot scale to our business model. Our machines share real commonality, which is why we have templates and standards, but every job is custom. That means there will always be a long tail of logic our rule set has not seen yet. Chasing that tail by continuously adding more deterministic rules has diminishing returns and no natural end point.

The fix is not a return to freeform AI code generation either, since that reintroduces the inconsistency problem we are trying to escape. The right model separates the pipeline into a deterministic interpreter stage and an AI reasoning stage, each doing only the work it is suited for.

1. State Logic Builder and Compiler stage, fully deterministicThe GUI captures the state logic, hardware, servo setpoints, and other front end parameters. A deterministic Python layer compiles this into a structured, human readable intermediate representation. This layer does not generate L5X. Its job is strictly interpretation and structuring: turning what the ME/CE entered into a well organized format the AI stage can reliably consume. The human readable output also gives our engineers a cheap, early point to review and catch errors during development, before anything reaches the AI stage.

2. L5X Generating LLM, the only stage that writes L5XTakes the structured intermediate representation and generates the actual L5X code, for every job, common patterns and custom logic alike. This is where reasoning happens: recognizing which known pattern applies, and applying engineering judgment where a job is genuinely custom. The instructions for this LLM will be developed as their own dedicated project, using a separate AI agent to interview us, ask clarifying questions, and co-developthe instruction set (a technique known as meta-prompting), rather than improvising prompts ad hoc as we have been doing.

We also plan a separate meta-prompting exercise focused specifically on the intermediate representation itself: working with an AI agent to determine what format and data the L5X generating LLM actually needs as input, before we lock in the schema.
3. Check and Correction Layers, mixed deterministic and AI judgmentRecommend three layers, each with a narrow, specific job:

text:list-item.text:p: Structural validation (deterministic): is the L5X well formed and schema valid.
Standards conformance (deterministic or lightweight AI): does it follow our written naming, tagging, and pattern rules.
Style and pattern match (AI, judgment based): does this look like what our engineers would actually write, checked against our golden examples.

office:text.text:p: Not every layer needs to be an AI call. Mixing deterministic and AI based gates keeps cost and latency down, reserving AI judgment for checks that genuinely require it.
Design Question: Should We Bake L5X "Shell" Code Into the Deterministic Layer?

We discussed whether the deterministic compiler stage should also generate partial L5X shell code (routine skeletons, standard rung shapes, AOI call structures) for the LLM to fill in, rather than leaving all code generation to the LLM. Conclusion: only where there is genuinely zero remaining ambiguity.

text:list-item.text:p: Good candidates for deterministic shell code: routine and program scaffolding, tag database structure, and standard AOI instantiation calls with parameters pulled directly from the intermediate representation. These are structural, not judgment calls.

Bad candidates: anything that looks standard on the surface but actually varies by context, such as a rung shape that differs by actuation type or a fault sequence whose structure depends on upstream station count. Baking in a wrong assumption as if it were settled fact is worse than leaving a gap, because it is harder to catch.

Practical test before baking anything in: have senior engineers try to break the "standard" pattern by thinking of a real job where it would not apply as is. If they cannot break it, it is safe to bake in. If they can, it belongs in LLM generated territory instead.

Important caveat: baking in shell code does not automatically reduce total verification work. If the shell still needs to be checked for applicability, we have added a step rather than removed one. It only pays off for patterns confident enough that verification becomes unnecessary.

office:text.text:p: Key Constraint: Our Example Library Is Small and Specific

We have hundreds of legacy PLC projects, but our actual "good" reference material is narrower: two template projects, covering two basic machine types, each containing example stations for some of our most common station designs. We do not have thirty examples, and we do not have many examples of similar but slightly different stations. What we do have is a number of genuinely golden examples for common station types.
This matters for how we build the AI's reference material:

text:list-item.text:p: Quality beats quantity for AI examples. Research on few shot prompting consistently shows that a small number of clean, well chosen examples outperforms a large set of mixed quality ones. Noisy examples measurably degrade output rather than simply failing to help. Feeding the AI our hundreds of legacy files directly risks teaching it our past inconsistencies as if they were the standard.

Our two templates are a strong starting core, not a finished library. They cover common station types well but leave gaps around near miss variations, stations that are similar to a golden example but different in some meaningful way. Those near miss cases are likely where our current generator struggles most, and where the LLM will need either more examples or stronger reasoning support.

Recommended near term deliverable: deliberately expand the golden set to cover near miss variations of our existing common stations, rather than trying to mine hundreds of legacy files for signal. This is a scoped, boundable project.

The legacy projectscouldstill have value in a supporting role: mining them to identify which near miss variations and less common station types actually recur (telling us what new golden examples to prioritize), and as a validation and regression set, testing new pipeline output against real historical requirements without letting the raw files influence generation directly.

The current Python L5X generator is not simply discarded. The design knowledge embedded in it (how our rung structures work, what our tag naming actually produces, which parameters map to which logic patterns) carries forward into thenew compiler stage's structuring logic and into the golden examples and instructions for the L5X generating LLM.

The new investment is: the structured intermediate representation (its own meta-prompting project), the instruction set project for the L5X generating LLM (including expanding the golden example set), and the validation and correction layers.

We should build a small test suite of representative state diagrams with known correct expected output, and version the instruction set like code, so we can tell whether a given change actually improved results rather than iterating by feel.

Fine tuning a model on our data is not recommended at this stage. It is expensive, requires a large curated dataset we do not have, and is harder to update as our standards evolve. The golden example plus instruction set approach gets most of the benefit at much lower cost and stays easy to revise.
